section.title: Disaster from the North
section.sectionRationale: The boiling pot vision of chapter 1 now becomes an urgent battle alarm. Jeremiah sounds the trumpet, describes an invading nation as a lion and a scorching wind, feels the coming disaster in his own body, and finally sees in vision the undoing of creation itself, judgment so severe it reverses Genesis.
section.thesis: The LORD is bringing an unstoppable invader from the north against Judah's covenant unfaithfulness, a judgment so total that Jeremiah pictures the created order itself unraveling back toward formlessness, yet even here the LORD will not make a full end.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the trumpet sounded and cities warned to flee; the scorching wind and the besieging nation described; Jeremiah's own anguish at what he sees; and the vision of uncreation, the earth returning to formless void.

units.label: Sound the alarm
units.note: the shofar, the signal flag, the lion from his thicket

verses.text:
Announce in Judah, proclaim in Jerusalem, and say: 
“Blow the {{shofar|ram's horn}} throughout the land. Cry aloud and say, ‘Assemble yourselves and let us flee to the fortified cities.’
Raise a signal flag toward Zion. Seek refuge! Do not delay! For I am bringing disaster from the north, and terrible destruction.
A lion has gone up from his thicket, and a destroyer of nations has set out. He has left his lair to lay waste your land. Your cities will be reduced to ruins and lie uninhabited.
So put on sackcloth, mourn and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned away from us.”
“In that day,” declares the LORD, “the king and officials will lose their courage. The priests will tremble in fear, and the prophets will be astounded.”
Then I said, “Ah, Lord GOD, how completely You have deceived this people and Jerusalem by saying, ‘You will have peace,’ while a sword is at our throats.”

units.label: The scorching wind
units.note: an army like clouds and whirlwind

verses.text: At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, “A searing wind from the barren heights in the desert blows toward the daughter of My people, but not to winnow or to sift;
a wind too strong for that comes from Me. Now I also pronounce judgments against them.”
Behold, he advances like the clouds, his chariots like the whirlwind. His horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, for we are ruined!
Wash the evil from your heart, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved. How long will you harbor wicked thoughts within you?
For a voice resounds from Dan, proclaiming disaster from the hills of Ephraim.
Warn the nations now! Proclaim to Jerusalem: “A besieging army comes from a distant land; they raise their voices against the cities of Judah.
They surround her like men guarding a field, because she has rebelled against Me,” declares the LORD.
“Your ways and deeds have brought this upon you. This is your punishment; how bitter it is, because it pierces to the heart!”

units.label: Jeremiah's anguish
units.note: my anguish, I cannot be silent

verses.text: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh, the pain in my chest! My heart pounds within me; I cannot be silent. For I have heard the sound of the horn, the alarm of battle.
Disaster after disaster is proclaimed, for the whole land is laid waste. My tents are destroyed in an instant, my curtains in a moment.
How long must I see the signal flag and hear the sound of the horn?
“For My people are fools; they have not known Me. They are foolish children, without understanding. They are skilled in doing evil, but they know not how to do good.”

units.label: Uncreation
units.note: formless and void, no light, no man, no birds

verses.text: I looked at the earth, and it was {{tohu_vabohu|formless and void}}; I looked to the heavens, and they had no light.

I looked at the mountains, and behold, they were quaking; 
all the hills were swaying.
I looked, and no man was left; all the birds of the air had fled.
I looked, and the fruitful land was a desert. All its cities were torn down before the LORD, before His fierce anger.

For this is what the LORD says: 
“The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction.
Therefore the earth will mourn and the heavens above will grow dark. I have spoken, I have planned, and I will not relent or turn back.”
Every city flees at the sound of the horseman and archer. They enter the thickets and climb among the rocks. Every city is abandoned; no inhabitant is left.

And you, O devastated one, what will you do, though you dress yourself in scarlet, though you adorn yourself with gold jewelry, though you enlarge your eyes with paint? You adorn yourself in vain; your lovers despise you; they want to take your life.

For I hear a cry like a woman in labor, a cry of anguish like one bearing her first child, the cry of the Daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands to say, “Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers!”

shofar.gloss: A ram's horn trumpet, used both to summon Israel to worship and to warn of approaching war. Its repeated sounding through this passage marks the shift from Jeremiah's private call to public, national alarm.

tohu_vabohu.gloss: Formless and void, the exact phrase used of the earth before creation in Genesis 1:2. Jeremiah deliberately reuses it here, picturing covenant judgment as a kind of undoing of creation itself, the land returned toward the chaos from which God first spoke order.

basic.context: Jeremiah sounds the battle alarm: an unnamed invader from the north is coming like a lion, like a scorching desert wind, like storm clouds, and no one, not king, priest, or prophet, will keep their nerve. Jeremiah himself is not a detached announcer; he feels the coming disaster in his own body, and in a devastating vision he sees the created world itself begin to unravel back toward the darkness and formlessness of Genesis 1:2.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic poetry describing a real coming military disaster, almost certainly the Babylonian invasions that would culminate in 586 BC, using cosmic and creational imagery to convey the theological weight of covenant judgment. The hard truth to sit with is verse 27, God will not make a full end, judgment here is real and severe, described in the most catastrophic language available, yet even at its worst it stops short of total annihilation.
basic.originalLanguages: The shofar sounds again and again, moving the alarm from private oracle to public emergency. When Jeremiah looks at the devastated land, he sees it as tohu vabohu, formless and void, the identical phrase used of the earth in Genesis 1:2 before God spoke light and order into being, so that covenant judgment is pictured as creation undone.
basic.typology: The reversal of creation here anticipates its opposite: the new creation promised throughout Scripture, where God speaks light, order, and life back into a ruined world through Christ. Jeremiah's own anguish, feeling in his body the judgment his people refuse to feel, anticipates the greater weeping and grief of Christ over Jerusalem.
basic.christ: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem in words that echo this very theme, if only you had known the things that make for peace, Luke 19:41-44, standing in the line of Jeremiah as a prophet who feels covenant judgment in His own body and grieves over a city's refusal to turn. Where Jeremiah's vision ends in near-total undoing, the gospel promises the reversal of that undoing, a new heaven and new earth, in Christ.
basic.god: God is both the author of this judgment, I have spoken, I have planned, and I will not relent, and the one who limits it, I will not finish its destruction. His anger against covenant unfaithfulness is severe enough to picture the unmaking of creation, yet His mercy still holds back total annihilation, keeping a future open beyond the disaster.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1:2 supplies the exact phrase, formless and void, that Jeremiah reuses to describe judgment. Luke 19:41-44 has Jesus weep over Jerusalem's coming destruction in language that echoes Jeremiah's own anguish. Zephaniah 1:2-3 pictures a similarly cosmic undoing of creation in judgment. Revelation 21:1-5 answers this undoing with the promise of a fully remade heaven and earth.
basic.oneStory: This is the alarm before the storm, a prophet who feels in his own body the judgment coming on a people who will not feel it themselves, pictured as creation itself unraveling. That undoing is not the last word of Scripture; it points forward to the new creation God will finally accomplish through Christ, where light, order, and life are spoken back into a ruined world for good.

context.literary:
The poem has no narrator in the usual sense. Voices cut across each other: a herald in 4:5, the LORD in 4:6 to 9, Jeremiah in 4:10, an anonymous speaker in 4:11 to 13, the LORD again in 4:14 to 18, Jeremiah in 4:19 to 21, the LORD in 4:22, the prophet's eye in 4:23 to 26, the LORD in 4:27 and 28, and then the unnamed crowd and the personified city in 4:29 to 31. The reader is not told who is speaking, and that is part of the effect. The disaster is too large for a single point of view.

The passage is tied together by sound as much as sense. Verses 5 and 6 are a rapid string of imperatives, blow, cry, assemble, flee, raise, seek refuge, do not delay. Then the verbs change. In 4:23 to 26 the poet writes the same clause four times, 'I looked', and each time the sentence sees a fresh layer of the world gone. First the earth, then the heavens, then the hills, then the people and birds, and finally the fruitful land and the cities. The repetition acts like a camera pulling slowly out from a house to a country to the world, and it empties each frame of life.

Within the larger book the passage is a deliberate answer to chapter 1. The pot of 1:13 and 1:14 now boils over, the word of the LORD that was 'watching' now moves, and the call to 'be a fortified city' contrasts with the people running to fortified cities, 4:5, who find no safety. It is also the first of several alarm poems that recur at 6:1 to 5 and 6:22 to 26 and 8:14 to 17, so that the book keeps returning to the northern threat.

The passage ends on a woman in labour, 4:31, a final image of the city gasping for breath. The birth-pain simile is picked up later in the book and made more tragic, because the labour here brings no birth. The last voice in the poem is not the prophet's or the LORD's but the city's own, 'Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers', so the poem ends with a cry that no one answers.
context.historical:
The language of the invasion belongs to a long tradition of curses. Deuteronomy 28:49 to 52 had said long before that the LORD would bring 'a nation from afar' to 'swoop down upon you like an eagle', a ruthless nation whose language the people would not understand. Jeremiah 5:15 repeats those very terms of 'a nation whose language you do not know'. The prophet is not inventing a threat but telling the people that the covenant curses are now being collected.

The date is the late seventh century. The oracle likely belongs to the early years of Josiah's reform or just after, when the Assyrian empire was collapsing and the Babylonians under Nabopolassar were rising from 626 BC. Egypt, under Pharaoh Neco, marched north in 609, and Josiah died trying to stop him, 2 Kings 23:29. In 605 Babylon defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish, Jeremiah 46:2, and Nebuchadnezzar's armies came down the coastal route. Jehoiakim became his vassal and then rebelled, 2 Kings 24:1. The first deportation came in 597 and the city fell in 586 BC, when the temple was burned and the walls broken down, Jeremiah 52:12 to 14.

The military images are those of a land that knew ancient warfare. The alarm was a ram's horn, the shofar, and a banner raised on a hill to signal danger. Villagers fled to walled towns, and Jeremiah 4:29 shows them fleeing instead to the thickets and the rocks as the whole system of defence breaks down. The 'horseman and archer' of 4:29 stand for the mounted attackers who scatter every town. Jeremiah 6:22 and 23 repeats the same pictures of spear, bow and mounted lines.

The woman in 4:30 puts on scarlet, gold and eye paint, and the details have a historical edge. This is the toilet of a royal or aristocratic woman, as when Jezebel painted her eyes just before her death, 2 Kings 9:30. Here the figure is Jerusalem, who has courted allies, Egypt and Assyria, and learns that her 'lovers' are now her killers.
context.canonical:
The creation reversal in 4:23 to 26 depends on Genesis 1. The pair 'formless and void' in verse 23 recalls the first condition of the earth in Genesis 1:2, and the successive removal of light, land, humanity and birds echoes the order of the creation days. The phrase has an echo in Isaiah 34:11, where the LORD stretches over Edom a line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction, again using the creation-undone language for a judged nation. Hosea 4:1 to 3 offers a sibling picture, in which the land mourns, and the beasts, birds and fish fade away because of human sin, and Zephaniah 1:2 and 3, written in the same reign, announces a sweeping away of man and beast, birds and fish. Genesis 6:7 had said the same of the flood.

The 'Day of the LORD' vocabulary also appears. Amos 5:18 to 20 warns that the day people long for will be darkness and not light, and Isaiah 13:9 and 10 describes the sun darkened and the stars not giving light. Zephaniah 1:14 to 16 speaks of a day of horn blast and battle cry against the fortified cities, nearly the language of Jeremiah 4:5 and 6. The line 'the whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction', 4:27, is repeated at 5:10 and 5:18 and in 30:11, and it forms the hinge of the whole book: there will be an end and there will not be an end.

The New Testament carries the pattern in two directions. Jesus takes the language of darkened sun and moon and shaken powers into His own teaching about the end, Mark 13:24 to 26 and Matthew 24:29, and He announces the destruction of the temple that Jeremiah had warned about, Mark 13:1 and 2. Peter and John see the dissolution of the heavens as leading to a new heaven and a new earth, 2 Peter 3:10 to 13, Revelation 6:12 to 14 and 21:1. Paul reads creation's present groaning as labour pains awaiting its release, Romans 8:19 to 22, which gives the birth-pain image of Jeremiah 4:31 a hopeful interpretation.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The passage was meant to break a national complacency. Judah's rulers and prophets had settled on a comfortable formula, 'You will have peace', 4:10, and the common people repeated it. Jeremiah's poem is designed to make that impossible. A herald blows the horn across the land, the prophet clutches his chest, the heavens go dark. The first hearers were meant to leave unable to say that they had not been warned.

It was also meant to teach them how to understand what was coming. The northern army is not a random scourge, 'a wind too strong for that comes from Me', 4:12. The LORD is the one who 'pronounces judgments', which is courtroom language. The disaster is the sentence of a judge who has first given a long hearing, and that is why 4:18 can say, 'Your ways and deeds have brought this upon you.' The author wants the people to read their history as a verdict and not as bad luck.

And it was meant to show them what a faithful messenger feels. Jeremiah does not stand outside the judgment like a news reporter. He writhes with it, and the book keeps him in the poem as a counterweight to the LORD's voice. A people who hear both the angry God and the grieving prophet are being shown that the judgment comes with sorrow. For the exiles, who would later read this, the passage said that the disaster had been foreseen and that the prophet had wept over it first.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what Jeremiah saw and heard and what the LORD announced about a particular invasion. It does not tell readers to expect the same events, and it should not be turned into a map of the current news. The cosmic images, the darkness and the quaking hills, are the poet's way of showing the size of a political catastrophe in a land whose whole world was its covenant. They are not a weather forecast, and the author does not claim that the physical heavens went dark in 586.

What does carry over is a set of instructions about how to hear warnings. Repent while there is time, 4:14, 'Wash the evil from your heart'. Do not trust a message that says all is well when the evidence says otherwise, 4:10. Take the grief of the messenger as seriously as the message. The text does not instruct anyone to treat their enemies as divinely appointed destroyers, and it does not say that every disaster is a judgment on its victims. Jesus rejects that inference in Luke 13:1 to 5, and the book of Jeremiah itself shows the righteous suffering along with the guilty.

debates.question: Who is the enemy from the north?

views.label: Babylon
views.case: Jeremiah names it later, 'Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon' and 'all the families of the north', 25:9, and the events of 605, 597 and 586 match the sequence of the book. The enemy here is described in the same terms as the Babylonian army in 6:22 and 6:23, and the north is the direction from which armies entered Judah, since the desert lay to the east and the sea to the west.

views.label: A Scythian or other nomad raid
views.case: Some older scholarship tied the early oracles to a northern raid mentioned by Greek historians, as the poem was composed early, in Josiah's reign, before Babylon was a threat. Evidence of such an invasion of Judah is thin, and most recent writers hold that the poems fit Babylon better.

views.label: A deliberately unnamed, mythic foe
views.case: The north was also the realm of the mysterious and dangerous in biblical thought. Some readers hold that the poem uses 'the north' as a symbol of any force the LORD summons, so that it could apply to a series of enemies. This reading explains why the poem's images are so general.

debates.bearing: The poem does not need the enemy named to do its work. What matters is verse 6, 'I am bringing disaster from the north', and the people who read it afterward saw it come true in Babylon.

debates.question: Does God change His mind, since 4:28 says 'I will not relent'?

views.label: The announcement was conditional, and here the condition is unmet
views.case: Jeremiah 18:7 to 10 sets the rule: when the LORD announces judgment and the nation turns, He relents; when He announces blessing and the nation does evil, He relents of that too. In 4:28 the people have shown they will not turn, so the sentence stands, which is why 4:14 still calls for repentance.

views.label: God's character does not change, though His dealings do
views.case: Numbers 23:19 says God is not a man that He should change His mind, yet the same Hebrew verb is used of God relenting in Jeremiah 18:8 and 26:3. Many theologians take the language as speaking from the human side: God's purposes and nature are fixed, and He acts differently toward people who change.

views.label: God genuinely responds in time
views.case: Others, including some who defend a view called open theism, take the passages at face value and say that God really does adjust His plans in response to human choices. They argue the book's repeated 'perhaps they will turn' in 26:3 and 36:3 would otherwise be empty.

debates.bearing: All three agree that in this poem the call to repent is serious and the judgment real. The question is how to speak of God's freedom in light of that.

study.originalLanguages:
The word the BSB renders 'disaster' in 4:6 and 'destruction' is shever, a breaking or fracture. It is the word for a broken bone or a shattered pot, and it begins a chain through the book. In 4:20 the BSB's 'Disaster after disaster' is literally shever upon shever. In 6:14 the BSB's 'wound' is shever again: the prophets treat the people's breaking as though it were a scratch. In 8:21 the BSB's 'brokenness' of the daughter of my people is shever once more, and Jeremiah says that he too is crushed. The same word thus names the army's work, the people's condition and the prophet's own heart.

In 4:7 the invader is 'a destroyer of nations', the Hebrew mashchit, a participle of the verb shachat, to ruin or corrupt. It is the word used for the destroyer that the LORD would not allow into Israelite homes at the Passover, Exodus 12:23. A word that once described the threat the blood protected against now describes what is coming to the house of the LORD's own people. The same verb of ruin also stands in Genesis 6:12, where the earth was corrupt, and in 6:13, where God says He will destroy it, so the link with the flood is verbal.

The statement in 4:12, 'I also pronounce judgments against them', uses the idiom of dibber mishpatim, speaking verdicts. It is the same phrase as in 1:16, where the LORD says He will 'pronounce My judgments' against the people for forsaking Him. The call of chapter 1 and the invasion of chapter 4 are two ends of one legal process.

In 4:22 the LORD calls the people foolish and says they are 'skilled in doing evil', and 'skilled' is the wise-man word. The Hebrew sets 'wise' against 'foolish', the vocabulary of Proverbs, so the verse says in effect: they are wise to do evil, and know not how to do good. It is an irony drawn from the schools. Jeremiah 8:7 follows with the stork that knows her season while the people do not know the LORD's requirements.

In 4:19 the BSB has 'My anguish'. The Hebrew is literally 'my insides', the seat of emotion, and the 'pain in my chest' is, in the Hebrew, 'the walls of my heart'. The prophet feels the alarm as a pounding in the chambers of his heart.

The creation language is the most important. Tohu, formless, and bohu, void, appear together in Genesis 1:2 and here, and nowhere else as a pair. Isaiah 34:11 separates the two words into 'a measuring line of chaos' and 'a plumb line of destruction', and Isaiah 45:18 says that God did not create the earth tohu, to be empty. The four-fold 'I looked' of verses 23 to 26 removes in turn the light that God made on the first day, the stable hills, the human being and the birds. The word the BSB renders 'fruitful land' in verse 26 is ha-karmel, the orchard land, a word for the very best of cultivated ground.

In 4:27 the Hebrew for 'finish' is kalah, a full end. The phrase is repeated in 5:10, 5:18 and 30:11, always as a limit set on judgment. In 4:28 the verb nacham, the BSB's 'relent', is the same verb that appears in Jeremiah 18:8 and 26:3 and, negated, in Numbers 23:19.

The eye makeup of 4:30 uses the word puk, paint, a dark powder for the eyelids. It occurs again in 2 Kings 9:30, where Jezebel paints her eyes before her death.

typology.fulfillment: The poem shows what judgment looks like when it is allowed to run, and the end of the story is its reverse. God promises new heavens and a new earth, Isaiah 65:17, and Peter and John see this come, 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1. The creation that groans in labour, Romans 8:19 to 22, will be set free through the children of God. The type is limited: Jeremiah's undoing falls on one land, whereas the new creation renews all things in Christ, Colossians 1:20.

A messenger who feels the blow that he announces. Jesus wept over Jerusalem as He approached the city, Luke 19:41, and said that He would have gathered her children as a hen gathers her chicks, Matthew 23:37. Where Jeremiah could only grieve with the people, Christ takes the judgment on Himself, bearing our griefs and carrying our sorrows, Isaiah 53:4. The prophet's tears foreshadow the Saviour's, though Jeremiah's could not save anyone.

The poem has the lights going out and the hills shaking, and at the cross the same signs appear: darkness over all the land from the sixth to the ninth hour, and the earth shaking as the rocks were split, Matthew 27:45 and 51. The correspondence is a resonance, not a prediction. At Calvary the judgment of the day of the LORD falls on the one who bears it. Jeremiah's vision falls on a land; the cross is where the whole weight of judgment is taken by a person.

typology.type: A remnant spared, 'I will not finish its destruction', Jeremiah 4:27
typology.fulfillment: The limit on judgment becomes visible in a preserved remnant, the survivors of the exile, and in the line from them to the Messiah. Paul reasons from this pattern that God has not rejected His people but keeps a remnant chosen by grace, Romans 11:1 to 5. The final preservation is the resurrection of Christ, the one who went through the full judgment and came out alive. The type falls short in that the exile's survivors were spared for a time, while those who are in Christ are spared for good.

study.christ:
Chapter 4 offers no direct sentence about the Messiah, but it leaves the reader in a place where nothing short of a Messiah would be adequate. The people are wise in evil, the nation is gone, even creation is returning to chaos. The question the poem leaves is what could ever put the world back.

The first answer is in the shape of the prophet. Jeremiah does not stand outside the judgment. 'My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain', 4:19, and 8:21 and 9:1 carry on in the same voice. The New Testament places Jesus in this tradition. He weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41 to 44, in words that recall Jeremiah's lament, and warns that the city will be levelled because it did not recognise the time of its visitation, which matches the unmistakable theme of Jeremiah 4:18. Jesus also speaks of the temple having not one stone left upon another, Mark 13:2, and says that its house will be left desolate, Matthew 23:38. Like Jeremiah, He is accused of treason for saying so, and like Jeremiah, He says it because He loves the city.

The second answer is in the reversal. The undoing of creation is a judgment, and the Christian hope is that what was undone is made again in Christ. Paul says that all things were created through Him and for Him, and that in Him all things hold together, Colossians 1:16 and 17, and then that God has reconciled to Himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20. Whoever is in Christ is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17. The light that Jeremiah saw extinguished is the light that shines in the darkness, which the darkness has not overcome, John 1:5, and the Spirit hovering over a formless world in Genesis 1:2 is the Spirit who raised Jesus and who will give life to the mortal bodies of His people, Romans 8:11.

The third answer is in the cross. The darkness of the sixth hour is the darkness the poem sees. Jesus cries that He has been forsaken, Matthew 27:46, and the language of Jeremiah 2:13 in which God is forsaken is reversed, since here the one who never forsook the LORD is forsaken in the place of those who did. This is not a hidden prophecy in Jeremiah 4. It is how the New Testament shows that the judgment poured out on the land in the prophet's day falls, finally, on the Son.

It would be a mistake to see every image as a hidden picture of Christ. The lion and the whirlwind are the Babylonians, not Jesus, and the poem should be allowed to be about the coming of the army. What it does is to leave an open wound and a question of how God will handle the damage of sin. The gospel is the New Testament's answer.
study.god:
The God of this passage is terrifying and the passage does not try to make Him less so. He says 'I am bringing disaster', 4:6, 'a wind too strong for that comes from Me', 4:12, and 'I have spoken, I have planned, and I will not relent or turn back', 4:28. The northern army moves at His word. This is not a God who is surprised by history or whose plans are overridden by the powers of the day. Amos 3:6 asks whether calamity comes to a city unless the LORD has caused it, and Jeremiah's poem takes the same view: the invader is only the instrument.

The same God is the Creator. The vision of 4:23 to 26 can undo the world only because the world is His to give and to take back. Light, hills, birds and the fruitful land are all unmade in the order of their making, and the text names no other power that does the unmaking. Isaiah 45:18 says that He did not create the earth to be empty but formed it to be inhabited, and so the return to chaos is not what He wanted for the world. It is what sin has earned. The judgment is carried out by the one who made the world and who could not stand to see it fouled.

He is also a God who limits what He does. 'The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction,' 4:27. In the middle of the most sweeping language in the book, the LORD says that the fire will stop. The hope is not described, and no one in the poem sees it, but the line stands as an anchor. Lamentations 3:22 says later that it is because of the LORD's loving devotion that 'we are not consumed'. The same God who ordains the disaster sets the boundary on it.

He is a God who feels. It is the prophet's voice, not the LORD's, in 4:19 to 21. Jeremiah's grief is not a private weakness, for he weeps in 13:17 over 'the LORD's flock' taken captive. But the prophet's grief belongs to a wider sorrow: in 12:7 the LORD Himself speaks of giving 'the love of My life' into the hands of her enemies. A God who plans the judgment and grieves over it is a mystery the text does not explain, and the reader is not asked to resolve it.

And He is a God who warns. The alarm sounds before the army arrives. 'Wash the evil from your heart, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved', 4:14, is the speech of a God who would rather not have to carry out the sentence. Second Chronicles 36:15 says that He sent word again and again 'because He had compassion on them'. Judgment is the last thing He chooses, and it comes only after the long mercy of warning.

For worship the passage requires fear in the right sense. It is the fear of a world that belongs to Someone and a conscience that answers to Him, and it is the beginning of wisdom, Proverbs 1:7. The people of 4:22, who are skilled at evil and ignorant of the LORD, are the picture of its absence. Worship that does not tremble at anything is not worship of this God, and worship that only trembles has not heard 4:27.

crossReferences.note: The earth 'formless and void' with darkness over the deep is the picture Jeremiah uses for the land under judgment. Reading the two together shows that Jeremiah is not borrowing a phrase but deliberately unmaking creation in the same order in which it was made.

Edom is given a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction, the same two words that Jeremiah joins in 4:23. It shows that the creation-undone image was available to the prophets as a way to describe the judgment of a nation.

The curse of a nation from afar that swoops like an eagle and speaks a language the people do not know sits behind Jeremiah's invader. Jeremiah's first hearers could have recognised the warning as the covenant sentence they had been told about.

Written in Josiah's reign, Zephaniah's announcement of a sweeping away of man and beast, birds and fish is the closest contemporary parallel to Jeremiah 4:23 to 26. Together they show that both prophets were drawing on a shared vision of judgment as the reversal of creation.
The land mourns, and beasts, birds and fish waste away because there is no knowledge of God in the land. It connects human sin with the unravelling of the created world, as Jeremiah does.

'Go up through her vineyards and ravage them, but do not finish them off.' Here the limit of 4:27 is repeated in the language of a vineyard. It is one of the refrains that stop the judgment short of annihilation.

The rule that governs God's announcements of judgment: if the nation turns, He relents. Reading it beside 4:28 shows why the same prophet can both promise that the LORD will not relent and plead with the people to turn.

Jeremiah's grief grows from the anguish of 4:19 into an unbroken lament, and he wishes that his eyes were a fountain of tears. It shows that 4:19 is not a passing mood but the settled posture of the prophet.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and says that her enemies will surround her and level her, because she did not recognise the time of her visitation. He speaks as one standing in Jeremiah's line, with the same sorrow and the same warning.

Jesus takes the darkened sun and moon and shaken powers of the Old Testament day of the LORD into His own teaching about the end. The language Jeremiah used of the fall of Jerusalem becomes the language for the final coming of the Son of Man.

Creation was subjected to futility and groans in labour until it is set free. The image of birth pains in Jeremiah 4:31 is turned from despair into hope, since the pangs lead to the freedom of the children of God.
John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the first passed away. What Jeremiah saw undone is made again, and the God who unmade it says that He is making all things new.

study.oneStory:
The whole Bible is a story about a world that was made well, spoiled, and will be made well again, and Jeremiah 4 is where the middle of that story is told with the lights out. Genesis 1 gives the order of creation: light, sky, land, plants, birds, humanity. Genesis 3 and 6 show how sin disturbs that order and how God, grieved, can wipe it back. The flood is the first uncreation, in which the waters that were separated are allowed to cover the earth again. Jeremiah 4:23 to 26 is the second, and it is aimed not at the whole world but at the one piece of it that was given to the LORD's people as the new Eden.

The land of Israel was meant to be a restored garden: a fertile land with a temple at the centre, a priestly people and the presence of God. The prophets knew this, which is why they describe its ruin in the language of Genesis 1. When the land goes dark, Eden is shut again. The exiles who read this poem understood that the loss of the land was a second expulsion from the garden, and the poem makes them hear it.

What it sets up is more than recovery. 'I will not finish its destruction' is the first thin thread of the hope that Jeremiah will weave in chapters 30 to 33, where the LORD promises to bring His people back, to plant them, and to make a new covenant. It leads on to Isaiah's new heavens and new earth, Isaiah 65:17, and to the claim of the New Testament that this is done in Christ. The one who weeps over the city and enters it on a donkey is also the one who goes through the judgment, in darkness at midday, and comes out alive.

The end of the story answers the poem line by line. Where Jeremiah looked and saw no light, John sees a city that has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God gives it light, Revelation 21:23. Where there was no man and the birds had fled, the nations walk by that light and the tree of life stands by the river, Revelation 22:2. Where the earth quaked and the hills swayed, the old order has passed away, and God Himself dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3 and 4. The labour pains of 4:31 turn out to be the labour of a world coming to birth, Romans 8:22, and the cry of the Daughter of Zion is answered by the voice from the throne, 'It is done', Revelation 21:6.

quiz.q: What image does Jeremiah use to describe the coming invader in verse 7?

options.text: A lion that has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations.
options.note: Verse 7 pictures the invader as a lion leaving its lair to lay waste the land.

options.text: A gentle shepherd bringing peace.
options.note: The passage describes violent destruction, the opposite of a gentle shepherd image.

options.text: A farmer bringing a harvest.
options.note: This is not the imagery used; the passage describes military devastation, not agricultural blessing.

options.text: A trading caravan from the east.
options.note: The invader is explicitly military and destructive, not a peaceful trading party.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah personally respond to the coming disaster in verses 19-21?

options.text: With physical anguish, writhing in pain and unable to stay silent.
options.note: Verse 19 shows Jeremiah feeling the coming judgment in his own body, not merely announcing it dispassionately.

options.text: With detached indifference toward his people's fate.
options.note: The text shows the opposite: deep personal anguish, not indifference.

options.text: With joy that his enemies will be punished.
options.note: Jeremiah's response is anguish and grief, not celebration.

options.text: By refusing to speak of it any further.
options.note: He explicitly says, I cannot be silent, continuing to proclaim the message despite his pain.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah see when he looks at the earth in verse 23?

options.text: The earth as formless and void, using the exact phrase from Genesis 1:2.
options.note: This deliberate echo pictures judgment as a kind of undoing of creation itself.

options.text: A newly built and thriving city.
options.note: The vision describes desolation and undoing, not new prosperity.

options.text: A peaceful and fruitful garden.
options.note: The vision is one of devastation, mountains quaking, no man, no birds, not a flourishing garden.

options.text: An image confined only to the temple building.
options.note: The vision describes the whole land and even the heavens, not merely the temple structure.

quiz.q: Despite the severity of this judgment, what limit does God set on it in verse 27?

options.text: The whole land will be desolate, but He will not make a full end.
options.note: Even amid the most severe judgment imagery in the passage, God explicitly limits the destruction.

options.text: The judgment will be reversed immediately with no consequences.
options.note: The passage describes real, severe desolation; it is limited, not avoided.

options.text: Only the northern tribes will be affected, not Judah.
options.note: The judgment explicitly targets Jerusalem and Judah throughout the passage.

options.text: The limit applies only to the enemy nation, not Judah itself.
options.note: The stated limit, I will not finish its destruction, refers to the land and people just described, Judah itself.

quiz.q: How does this passage anticipate the New Testament?

options.text: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem's coming judgment, echoing Jeremiah's own anguish, and Revelation promises a new creation reversing this undoing.
options.note: Luke 19:41-44 and Revelation 21:1-5 both connect meaningfully to this passage's themes of prophetic grief and creation's undoing and restoration.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The connections to Jesus' weeping over Jerusalem and to new creation are direct and substantial.

options.text: It only relates to end-times prophecy about literal astronomical events.
options.note: The connection is theological and typological, about judgment and new creation, not primarily literal astronomy.

options.text: It is fulfilled entirely within the Old Testament and has no further significance.
options.note: While it addresses Jeremiah's own historical moment, its creation-reversal imagery carries forward into New Testament hope of new creation.

questions: Jeremiah feels the coming judgment in his own body rather than announcing it with detachment. Where do you tend to keep hard truths at arm's length instead of letting them affect you honestly?
The invading disaster is described as unstoppable, like a lion, like a scorching wind. What in your life feels unstoppable right now, and how does trusting God change how you face it?
Jeremiah's vision pictures creation itself unraveling under judgment. Where have you seen sin's consequences unravel something good that God originally intended for flourishing?
Even at its most severe, God says He will not make a full end. Where do you need to trust God's restraint and mercy in the middle of real consequences you are facing?
Jesus later wept over Jerusalem in words that echo this very passage. What would it look like for you to grieve honestly over sin, your own or your community's, the way both Jeremiah and Jesus did?

translationNotes.note: Jeremiah's charge, You have deceived this people, is a striking accusation against God; many read this as Jeremiah voicing the people's own confusion at the false prophets' message of peace, rather than a literal claim that God lied.
Formless and void, tohu wa-bohu, occurs in the Hebrew Bible as this exact paired phrase only here and in Genesis 1:2, making the allusion to creation's original state unmistakable to Hebrew readers.

The address to the devastated one dressed in scarlet pictures Jerusalem as a woman applying cosmetics and finery in a futile attempt to attract the very lovers, foreign powers, who will bring about her ruin.
